title: Leviticus
subtitle: Be holy, for I am holy
lead: Leviticus is called in Hebrew Vayikra, "And he called," after its first word: the LORD called to Moses from the tent of meeting, the tent that had just been filled with his glory at the end of Exodus. The whole book is set in one place, at the foot of Sinai, and almost all of it is God speaking. It answers one question: how can a holy God live among an ordinary, mortal, sinning people without destroying them? Its English name, from the Greek, means "about the Levites," though it is mostly about the priests and the people.

Chapters 1–7 teach the five kinds of offering. Chapters 8–10 ordain Aaron and his sons, show the glory of the LORD accepting the first sacrifices, and tell how two of Aaron's sons died for bringing "strange fire." Chapters 11–15 set out clean and unclean: food, childbirth, skin disease and bodily discharges. Chapter 16, the Day of Atonement, stands at the center. Chapters 17–26, often called the Holiness Code, widen holiness from the sanctuary to the whole of life: blood, sex, justice for the poor and the foreigner, "love your neighbor as yourself" (19:18), the priests, the feasts, the Sabbath year and the Jubilee, ending in blessings and curses. Chapter 27 adds the rules for vows.

Many readers find Leviticus the hardest book of the Bible to love. It was also, traditionally, the first book Jewish children were taught, and it is the source of Yom Kippur, kashrut, and the command Jesus called second only to loving God. The New Testament letter to the Hebrews is in large part a commentary on it.
facts: Not named. Jewish and Christian tradition: Moses. Most critical scholars: priestly writers (P), with the Holiness school (H) responsible for chapters 17–26 and some other passages.
Set in the year after the exodus, at Sinai (Exodus 40:17; Numbers 1:1). Critical: priestly material from the late monarchy to after the exile, though many rituals are much older.
At the foot of Mount Sinai, at the tent of meeting
Ritual and moral law given as speeches from God, with narrative in chapters 8–10 and 24:10–23

audience.to: The book presents itself as the LORD's words through Moses to two groups camped at the foot of Mount Sinai, a year after leaving Egypt. One is Aaron and his sons, the newly ordained priests. The other is all the Israelites, with the foreigners living among them. Some speeches are for the priests alone, some for the whole people, and a few for both together (17:2; 22:18). On most critical views, its first readers were the priests and people of Judah who worshiped at the Temple in Jerusalem. Some place them in the late monarchy, others among exiles and returned exiles in the Persian period.
audience.why: To answer one problem: how a holy God can live in the middle of an ordinary, mortal, sinning people without the people being destroyed. Chapters 1–16 give the priests and the people what they need for the sanctuary. They cover offerings, the ordination of priests, clean and unclean, and the yearly Day of Atonement. Chapters 17–26 carry holiness out into the home, the field, the market, the calendar and the land to come. Chapter 27 rules on vows. Knowing who is addressed changes the reading. A law spoken to Aaron and his sons is a priest's manual, not a rule for every household. A law spoken to all Israel makes every farmer, judge and parent responsible for holiness. For readers after the land was lost, chapter 26 explained the exile and promised that God would remember his covenant.
views: Jewish and Christian tradition: Moses received these laws at Sinai for the Israelites in the camp, and wrote them down for them and for later generations in the land. Conservative scholars such as Wenham point to the camp, the tent and the wilderness rites. They also note that no king and no Jerusalem are mentioned.

Kaufmann, Haran, Hurvitz and Milgrom: the priestly laws were written before the exile, in the time of the First Temple, for its priests and worshipers. Hurvitz argued that their Hebrew is older than Ezekiel's.
The exile and the Second Temple

Wellhausen and many later critics: the priestly code was written during or after the exile for the community rebuilding Jerusalem, and the tent in the wilderness stands for the Temple. On this view the book gave a small people under Persian rule a holy center and a way of life.

Knohl and Milgrom: an older priestly Torah (P) spoke mainly to priests about the sanctuary. A later Holiness school (H) wrote chapters 17–26 and passages such as 11:43–45 and 16:29–34, and it addressed all Israel and the land. On this view the shift in audience is itself part of the book's history.

lenses.name: Law from Sinai
lenses.desc: The traditional Jewish and Christian reading: God gave these laws to Moses at Sinai for Israel's worship and life, as the book says. Defended today by scholars such as Gordon Wenham and Roy Gane.

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Most academic scholars read Leviticus as the work of priestly schools (P, and the Holiness Code H in 17–26), written down late in the monarchy or after the exile, though some rituals are old. Jacob Milgrom and Israel Knohl are leading voices.

lenses.name: Purity and symbol
lenses.desc: Anthropologists and many interpreters, following Mary Douglas, read the food, body and purity laws as a symbolic map of order, wholeness, life and death, rather than as hygiene or arbitrary rules.

lenses.name: Jewish tradition
lenses.desc: The rabbis made Leviticus the first book children studied. The Sifra, the Talmud, Rashi, Ramban and Maimonides read it as living law: kashrut, Yom Kippur, and prayer and study in place of sacrifice after the Temple fell.

lenses.name: Christian
lenses.desc: The church reads the sacrifices and the priesthood as fulfilled in Christ (Hebrews 7–10), and has long debated which laws still bind: the moral, ritual and civil division (Aquinas, Calvin), and Acts 10 and 15 on food and Gentiles.

The text page beside each chapter can show several translations. Only the one you pick is loaded.

Plain English

A fresh rendering made for this site from the Hebrew Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex), at about an 8th-grade reading level, drafted line by line from the Hebrew words and then put into natural English order, rather than adapted from another English version. YHWH is "the LORD." The technical words of the sacrifices are kept steady so a reader can follow them: "burnt offering," "grain offering," "peace offering," "sin offering" and "guilt offering"; "offering by fire"; "a soothing smell to the LORD"; and "make atonement" for kipper. The general word korban, "what is brought near," is "offering" throughout, as in Exodus and Numbers, and the verb hiqriv is "present." The worshiper "leans" his hand on the animal's head and "slaughters" it; the priests "splash" its blood against the altar or "spatter" it with a finger; the handful burned from a grain offering is the "token portion." Bene Yisra'el is "the Israelites," and an animal fit for the altar is "flawless." Hebrew idioms that would mislead in English, such as "if his hand does not reach" for "if he cannot afford," are made plain in the text and kept in the notes and word glosses. The lid of the ark is the "atonement lid." Tsara'at is "skin disease" in people and "mold" in cloth and houses, not "leprosy" (see 13:2). Azazel is left as a name (16:8). The day of fasting is the day to "humble yourselves" (16:29; 23:27), and 19:18 reads "love your neighbor, like yourself." Verse numbers follow English Bibles. They differ from the Hebrew in chapters 5–6: English 6:1–7 are Hebrew 5:20–26, and English 6:8–30 are Hebrew 6:1–23.

Where the Masoretic Text differs from the Samaritan Pentateuch, the Septuagint or the Dead Sea Scrolls in a way that matters, the variant is shown beside the verse, for example the "strange fire" the Greek adds at 16:1, and a longer reading at 15:3 shared by the Septuagint and a Qumran scroll.

KJV, ASV, WEB, YLT

Public-domain English versions. The KJV (1611, standard text of 1769) prints words the translators added in italics. Young's Literal Translation (1898) keeps Hebrew word order and tenses.

BSB

The Berean Standard Bible, a modern translation released into the public domain.

Hebrew

The Leningrad Codex (about AD 1008), as edited by the Westminster Leningrad Codex project and corrected in STEPBible's TAHOT (Tyndale House, Cambridge), with each word's meaning and grammar.

Leviticus is a map of space. At its center is the inner room of the tent, where God is present above the atonement lid; around it the tent, the courtyard and altar, the camp, and outside the camp the wilderness. People and things move between zones: holy and ordinary, clean and unclean (10:10). Sacrifice, purity and the Day of Atonement are ways of keeping the map in order so that God can stay. The second half carries the map outward, to the household, the field, the market, the calendar and the land.

Read for the refrains. "The LORD spoke to Moses" marks each new speech. "It is a soothing smell for the LORD" closes the burnt offerings; "the priest will make atonement for him, and he will be forgiven" closes the sin offerings. "I am the LORD" punctuates chapter 19. "Be holy, for I am holy" (11:44; 19:2; 20:26) is the book's motto. Notice also where the book breaks its pattern: the only stories (10:1–7; 24:10–23) both end in death, and both show what happens when the holy is treated carelessly.

The book's structure has been read as a ring with chapter 16 at its center, or as two halves, the holiness of the sanctuary (1–16) and the holiness of the people (17–27). Mary Douglas compared its plan to the layout of the tabernacle itself.

sections.b: Readers come to Leviticus with modern ideas of sacrifice as loss and of impurity as dirt or guilt. The book's own categories differ. A sacrifice is first a gift brought near to God, often a meal shared with him and with the priests. The "sin offering" deals with uncleanness as well as unintended sin, which is why a mother after childbirth brings one (12:6), and many scholars, following Jacob Milgrom, call it the "purification offering": its blood cleanses the sanctuary that Israel's sins and impurities have polluted. Others (Roy Gane, Jay Sklar, N. Kiuchi) argue that it also cleanses and ransoms the offerer. The verb kipper has been explained as "cover," "wipe off" and "ransom"; the book may use all three senses. Uncleanness is not sin: it comes from birth, death, sex, disease and certain animals, and it is cured by time and washing, but it must be kept away from the holy. The notes on 1:4, 4:3, 4:20, 11:47, 12:2, 13:2 and 16:8 give the main views.

sections.b: In the synagogue Leviticus is Torat Kohanim, "the instruction of the priests," and its earliest commentary, the Sifra, bears that name. Children once began their study with it: "Let the pure come and study purity" (Leviticus Rabbah 7:3). The Mishnah and Talmud devote whole orders to its sacrifices (Kodashim) and purity laws (Tohorot). After the Temple fell in AD 70, the rabbis taught that prayer, study of the sacrifices, acts of love and repentance take their place (Avot de-Rabbi Natan 4; Menachot 110a). Leviticus still shapes Jewish life through kashrut (chapter 11), the laws of family purity (15; 18:19), Yom Kippur (16; 23), the festivals (23) and the ethical heart of chapter 19, which Rabbi Akiva called "a great principle of the Torah." Modern Jewish scholars, notably Jacob Milgrom and Baruch Levine, have led the academic study of the book.

The early church read the book through Christ. Hebrews 7–10 sets Jesus as the high priest who "offered himself" once for all, entering the true holy place (Hebrews 9:11–12), and calls the old system a "shadow" (Hebrews 10:1). Paul calls Christ the hilastērion, the word the Greek uses for the atonement lid (Romans 3:25). Mark 7:19 and Peter's vision in Acts 10 were read as ending the food laws, and the Jerusalem council (Acts 15) asked Gentile believers to keep only a few laws that echo Leviticus 17–18. Origen's homilies on Leviticus read it as allegory of the soul. Medieval and Reformation theology divided the law into moral, ceremonial and civil parts, keeping the first, counting the second fulfilled and the third as Israel's own (Aquinas; Calvin; the Westminster Confession). Today the book is central to Christian debates over sexuality, the use of the Old Testament in ethics, and the Jubilee as a model for debt relief.

sections.b: Leviticus is among the best-preserved books of the Hebrew Bible. More than a dozen manuscripts were found at Qumran and Masada, several in the old paleo-Hebrew script (1QpaleoLev, 2QpaleoLev, 6QpaleoLev and the large 11QpaleoLev-a), others in the square script (4QLev-b, c, d, e, g), and two in Greek (4QLXXLev-a and 4QpapLXXLev-b). They agree closely with the Masoretic Text. The differences that do appear are small: a phrase lost or added, a pronoun changed, readings sometimes shared with the Samaritan Pentateuch or the Septuagint. The Septuagint of Leviticus is a careful, fairly literal translation. On this site the variants are reported from the standard editions and studies (the Dead Sea Scrolls Bible, Tov, Wevers, Freedman and Mathews, and Milgrom's commentary); not every reading could be checked against the manuscripts directly, and where a reading is reported only secondhand the note says so.

reading: The fullest commentary ever written on the book, a lifetime's work by a Jewish scholar; source of the "purification offering" and "ritual detergent" views.
Gordon J. Wenham, The Book of Leviticus (New International Commentary on the Old Testament, 1979)
A clear evangelical commentary that takes the book's symbolism and its Christian use seriously.
Compact Jewish commentary with the Hebrew text, strong on terms and ancient Near Eastern parallels.
Mary Douglas, Purity and Danger (1966) and Leviticus as Literature (1999)
The anthropologist's classic theory of the food and purity laws, and her later rethinking of it.
Jonathan Klawans, Impurity and Sin in Ancient Judaism (2000)
Distinguishes ritual from moral impurity, with a clear map of the debates from Leviticus to the New Testament.
A detailed challenge to Milgrom on what the purification offering and the Day of Atonement cleanse.
A short, readable commentary for beginners, by the author of Sin, Impurity, Sacrifice, Atonement.
The case that the Holiness school edited the Priestly Torah, changing the book's picture of God and holiness.
How Leviticus arranges space, people, time and rituals in degrees of holiness.

spec.title: Leviticus as a book about coming near
spec.body: My own reading of the whole book: Leviticus turns on the verb qarav, "come near, bring near." Its first command is "when any one of you brings near an offering" (1:2, where the Plain English says "presents"), and korban, "offering," means "what is brought near." The priests are "those who come near me" (10:3), and their sons die because they came near wrongly (16:1). The purity laws decide who may come near the holy and who must stay outside the camp; chapter 18 forbids "coming near" to close relatives; chapter 21 bars a priest with a defect from coming near to offer. The book is a grammar of approach: every law answers how near, by whom, with what, and when. Read this way, Hebrews' call to "come near with a genuine heart" (Hebrews 10:22) and the Jewish word for sacrifice, korban, both keep the book's central idea. The pattern has been noticed before: access to God is a common theme in commentaries (Wenham; Sklar), and Milgrom and Levine discuss qarav as a technical term. Building the whole book's structure around the verb is my suggestion.

authorship: Again and again the book says "the LORD spoke to Moses," and it ends "These are the commands that the LORD gave Moses for the Israelites on Mount Sinai" (27:34). Jewish and Christian tradition took Moses as its writer, and Jesus refers to the offering for skin disease as what "Moses commanded" (Mark 1:44). Conservative scholars such as Gordon Wenham, Roy Gane and Jay Sklar point to the book's wilderness setting (the camp, the tent, the goat sent into the desert), to rituals with second-millennium parallels in Hittite and Ugaritic texts, and to the absence of any mention of Jerusalem or a king.

In the Documentary Hypothesis Leviticus belongs wholly to the Priestly source, the latest of the four, usually dated to the exile or after (Wellhausen, 1878). Wellhausen argued that a law so concerned with one central sanctuary and a high priest reflects the Second Temple, and that the tabernacle is the temple projected back into the desert.

Many scholars, especially in Israel, date P earlier. Yehezkel Kaufmann, Menahem Haran, Avi Hurvitz and Jacob Milgrom argued that P's Hebrew is older than Ezekiel's (Hurvitz's linguistic studies), that Ezekiel quotes Leviticus 26, that P knows nothing of Ezekiel's demotion of the Levites as a punishment (Ezekiel 44:10–14), and that P gives the tithe to the Levites (Numbers 18:21) rather than to the priests, as later Second Temple practice often did (Josephus; Judith 11:13; Hebrews 7:5). On this view the priestly laws were written in the time of the First Temple, perhaps in the 700s BC.

Since August Klostermann (1877) chapters 17–26 have been called the Holiness Code, for their refrain "be holy, for I am holy." Israel Knohl and Jacob Milgrom argued that H is not an older code taken into P but a later priestly school that edited P and added passages elsewhere (for example 11:43–45 and 16:29–34), widening holiness from the priests to all Israel and the land.
